title: I Walk Into Every Quarterly Meeting Wanting To Be Tony Robbins. Heres What Actually Happens
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder explores the reality of developing people through high-stakes quarterly reviews where underperformance is made visible and confronted directly. The quarterly structure compels outcome-focused accountability without excuses: did you hit your goal or not? Then why? The discomfort people experience having to state missed targets publicly is not a problem but the entire point—it signals something real is happening, and those who sit in the discomfort, own it, and commit to change are the ones who grow. Those who deflect and externalize reveal patterns that predict how they'll respond to business crises. Mulder acknowledges the art of feedback timing: knowing when to ask the hard question that would crack someone open versus when to let the relationship develop more trust first. She admits she doesn't always get it right; sometimes she leaves meetings knowing she left something important unsaid. The quarterly meeting functions as both planning and diagnostic tool, and her role is imperfect: she's not always the brilliant coach but rather a leader trying to read the room well enough to say what actually helps. The practice is ongoing accountability, direct naming of hard truths, and building trust over time to deepen what people can hear.
points: Outcomes-focused quarterly accountability creates productive discomfort; when people must state unmet goals clearly to peers, some grow through accountability clarity while others reveal patterns of deflection that predict future performance problems.

The art of direct leadership is reading when to ask the hard question and when to let a relationship develop more trust first; timing the feedback for maximum receptiveness requires knowing the individual and the room.
Visible underperformance acknowledged in the room is clarifying and catalyzes growth; hiding failures perpetuates them and signals that standards are negotiable.
Defensive deflection patterns observed in meetings mirror how people respond to real business challenges; accountability meetings are diagnostic tools for identifying who can face failure directly.
Personal discomfort with difficult feedback delivery is part of the job; a leader's nervousness about reaction shouldn't prevent naming hard truths.
quotes: The discomfort in the room is not a sign that something is wrong. It's a sign that something real is happening. A meeting where everyone is comfortable is a meeting where nothing is being said that actually matters.
The ones who can sit in it and who can say clearly, this didn't happen and here's what I think got in the way and here's what I'm going to do differently? Those are the ones who grow. Every time.

The ones who can't sit in it, who deflect, who explain, who find the external reason before they find the internal one are the ones I watch carefully. Because that pattern in a meeting is the same pattern that shows up when something goes wrong in the business.

That judgment call of when to push and when to give it more time is the part of developing people that no framework fully captures. It requires knowing the person. Knowing the room. Knowing what they can hear right now versus what they'll be able to hear in six months.
You're not always Tony Robbins. Sometimes you're just a leader trying to read the room well enough to say the thing that actually helps.
The meeting is a diagnostic as much as it is a planning session.” Archived from Summer Mulder Substack on May 3, 2026 by Tim.
